title: KV bandwidth sleuthing lab journal
body:
Purpose:
Quick, rough lab journal capturing an exploratory run to correlate memory-channel bandwidth activity with KV cache eviction/reuse behavior. Trying to capture signals we haven't seen explained by simple hit/miss ratios (tail latencies, eviction waves). This is messy — notes to self + data + next steps.

Summary of hypothesis:
- Observed: transient eviction waves + spike in tail-latency that coincide with sustained (>200 ms) multi-request windows.
- Hypothesis: During certain multi-tenant mixes the GPU memory channel(s) saturate for short bursts, causing slower page fill/drain and increased KV eviction churn (lower reuse for hot keys) because the pageback/prefetch pipeline stalls.
- Sub-hypothesis: NVMe paging isn't the primary cause for short bursts (latency too high), it's HBM/DRAM channel contention and PCIe DMA stalls when concurrent big-key lookups plus prefetch threads run.

Workloads used:
- chat-short: seq-len 64, 2k reqs/s synthetic with single-token step profile, mix of cache-hit bias ~70% (prefetch enabled)
- chat-long: seq-len 1024, single-user synthetic, warm KV working set ~1.3M keys
- rerank-burst: synchronous embedding/rerank path that forces KV reads for context windows; bursts of 500 qps for 10s every 60s
- background-bandwidth-hog: synthetic DMA client that issues large contiguous reads across HBM/DRAM to simulate channel saturation (used to reproduce the effect)

Key experiments and observations:
1) Baseline (no hog):
- reuse-rate (hotset 1k keys window): 84%
- eviction-rate: ~12 evictions/min per worker
- avg-kv-read-latency (cold path): 2.5ms, hot-path in-cache: 0.4ms
- aggregate memory bandwidth (perf counters): ~420 GB/s sustained on node during peak, HBM theoretical ~900 GB/s (note: measured across two GPUs via nvidia-smi sampling)

2) Add background-bandwidth-hog (single host):
- reuse-rate dropped to 59% for same workload window (hotness collapsed for a subset of keys)
- eviction-rate jumped to ~38 evictions/min per worker (spiky)
- read-latency hot-path increased to 0.9ms; cold-path to 6.8ms
- measured instantaneous bandwidth spikes >700 GB/s on one GPU channel for short bursts (50–200ms) — correlates with eviction spikes
- tail 99.9th latency for requests increased from ~35ms to 210ms during bursts

3) Isolate PCIe vs HBM:
- repeated test with hog limited to GPU-local HBM reads (no PCIe traffic) -> same pattern (eviction wave)
- repeated test with heavy PCIe transfers (peer DMA) but not hogging HBM -> smaller effect: reuse-rate ~75%
- inference: HBM/dram channel contention is main culprit, PCIe adds but not the primary cause

Profiling & tools used:
- perf counters exposing HBM read/write counters sampled via nvidia-smi + Nsight traces for narrow windows
- custom telemetry: per-key last-access timestamp, eviction timestamp, and a per-worker eviction-counter histogram (10s buckets)
- flamegraphs of worker main loop during bursts (sampled at 1kHz) — hotspots shift from decode/kv-hit-path to stall paths in prefetch and pageback logic during bursts
- linux perf and iostat show negligible NVMe activity during the sub-second bursts (so not disk-limited)

Interesting micro-observations:
- Eviction waves often have a 2-phase shape: initial sharp spike (keys evicted aggressively), then a slower sweep as background reclamation threads attempt to refill caches. The initial spike aligns with the peak HBM bandwidth windows.
- Prefetch threads sometimes pile up work; if their dequeue latency increases (because the memory channel is slower), they push more pages into the pageback queue causing synchronous eviction pressure.
- Certain key sizes are more sensitive: keys with large value blobs (model KV shards > 8KB) lead to higher bandwidth pressure per operation and amplify the effect.
- Multi-tenant mixes with 1 noisy tenant doing long seqlen generate enough sustained HBM time that short bursts of other tenants are evicted.

Quick sample telemetry snippet (aggregated):
- time=2024-09-25T15:12:34Z, bandwidth=742GB/s, reuse_rate=61%, evictions_bucket_10s=45, tail_latency_99_9=198ms
- time=2024-09-25T15:13:10Z, bandwidth=398GB/s, reuse_rate=83%, evictions_bucket_10s=9, tail_latency_99_9=37ms

Conclusions so far (work-in-progress):
- Short, high-amplitude HBM bandwidth bursts correlate strongly with eviction churn and tail latency increases.
- The existing eviction policy is too reactive for these short bursts: it assumes slower-changing access patterns and uses heuristics tuned for longer tail windows.
- Prefetch logic can worsen the problem: when prefetch latency increases, more speculative IO is queued causing additional pressure.

Immediate mitigation experiments to try next:
- Add a minimal bandwidth-aware admission control: if sampled instantaneous HBM bandwidth > X% of nominal, throttle prefetch submission rate for 100–500ms windows. Rationale: reduce speculative inflight pages and flatten the initial spike.
- Introduce sized-aware admission: deprioritize prefetches for keys with >8KB values when bandwidth is constrained.
- Smooth eviction algorithm: add a short refractory period (100–200ms) after a major eviction burst to avoid sweep-surge.
- Try lightweight per-tenant bandwidth quotas to prevent a single tenant from monopolizing channels in mixed deployments.

Data collection improvements (TODO):
- Capture per-channel HBM counters with tighter sampling (10ms) around known bursts. Need kernel-level hooks or vendor perf APIs for this.
- Correlate KV-level churn to GPU SM stall counters to confirm stall cause.
- Add microbench that exercises variable key-size distributions to map sensitivity curve (keysize vs eviction amplification).

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why do some bursts self-resolve quickly while others trigger longer sweeps? Hypothesis: threshold-crossing in prefetch queue depth and background compaction interplay. Need to instrument queue lengths end-to-end.
- Is there a hardware scheduling knob or kernel parameter that can reduce the worst-case instantaneous bandwidth peaks? (Vendor ask to infra team.)
- Could quantization/packing reduce bandwidth per key enough to avoid the pathology for typical models? (Needs workload-specific eval)

Action items (owner tags inline):
- [Maya] Implement a toggleable prefetch-throttle prototype in lab branch (rt/prefetch-throttle) and run 48h soak with mixed tenant profiles.
- [Arjun] Add 10ms HBM-sample harness using vendor perf API and validate with synthetic hog to ensure we can capture 10–50ms spikes.
- [Lena] Extend telemetry to include per-key size distribution and mark keys >8KB in histograms.
- [Samir] File infra ticket to verify if host kernel or driver settings can smooth DMA bursts (JIRA-RT-1122 follow-up).

Notes to self:
- Keep CSV dumps of per-bucket eviction histograms for the next meeting. Visualizing as heatmaps across time (10s x 1h) made patterns obvious in the initial run.
- Don't assume NVMe = cause for every long tail; this case looks HBM-bound for short bursts.

References and attachments:
- linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/456 (proto prefetch logging)
- Jira: JIRA-RT-1122 (investigate host/driver DMA throttling options)
- Confluence stub: CONFLUENCE-RT-BW-2024 (shared notes and graphs)

Meeting sync suggested: weekly 30m until prototype throttle shows reduction in eviction amplitude. Include bench output and 10ms HBM traces in agenda.

End of entry.
